# 3D Texture Mapping

Also called: 3D-Texture Volume Rendering, Rendering Slices with 3D Texture Mapping, Voltx Method, Volume Rendering with Shading via Three-Dimensional Texture Maps, Volume Texturing

## Overview
3D Texture Mapping is a hardware-accelerated [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) technique that projects the volumetric dataset onto parallel planar polygons (slices) and relies on the GPU's texture engine to perform trilinear interpolation and resampling [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial]. It solves the performance bottleneck of software-based [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) by offloading the computationally intensive sample evaluation to fixed-function hardware, rendering the volume in a ray-parallel fashion [S4]. Unlike sibling methods that may use [custom hardware units](#8284-custom-hardware-units.md) or specialized [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structures, this approach leverages standard 3D texture mapping capabilities available in graphics pipelines, often requiring pre-computed gradients or multi-pass techniques for shading [Parent].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family implement the emission-absorption optical model defined in [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md). The core pipeline for each pixel consists of ray generation, hardware-accelerated sampling, classification, and [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].

1.  **Ray Generation**: Rays are generated per-pixel, typically by computing ray parameters from camera matrices in vertex/fragment shaders or by rendering the volume's bounding box geometry to determine entry/exit points [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
2.  **Hardware-Accelerated Sampling**: Scalar volume values are sampled using the GPU's texture hardware. The volume data is stored in 3D texture memory, and the texture engine performs trilinear interpolation of the eight surrounding voxels in parallel, avoiding manual shader interpolation [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].
3.  **Fragment Shader Compositing**: The [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) loop, including classification and front-to-back compositing, is executed within the fragment shader [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md]. The standard compositing equation updates accumulated color $C'$ and opacity $\alpha'$:
    $$
    C'_{i} = C'_{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'_{i-1}) \alpha_i C_i
    $$
    $$
    \alpha'_{i} = \alpha'_{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'_{i-1}) \alpha_i
    $$
4.  **Early Ray Termination (ERT)**: Rays are terminated when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0) to optimize performance [5616-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering.md].

## Subtopics

### [Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering via 3D Texturing](2799-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering-via-3d-texturing.md)
The foundational technique that maps volume data to 3D textures and renders parallel slices. It distinguishes itself by using object-space or image-space polygon alignment strategies and hardware accumulation for resampling [2799-hardware-accelerated-volume-rendering-via-3d-texturing.md].

### [3D Pixel Texture Classification](6055-3d-pixel-texture-classification.md)
Extends the basic mapping by encoding a [3D transfer function](#5777-3d-transfer-function.md) (Data Value, Gradient Magnitude, Second Derivative) into a single texture lookup. It sets itself apart by integrating boundary-aware classification directly into the hardware sampling pipeline [6055-3d-pixel-texture-classification.md].

### [Hardware Shading via Pixel Texture](6056-hardware-shading-via-pixel-texture.md)
Adds surface shading to the volume rendering by storing quantized normals in a separate 2D pixel texture. It differs from siblings by using [nearest-neighbor interpolation](#5891-nearest-neighbor-interpolation.md) on this 2D texture to avoid truncation errors associated with interpolating normals [6056-hardware-shading-via-pixel-texture.md].

## Background
The method originated with the "Voltx" system developed at Silicon Graphics (SGI) in the mid-1990s, specifically for the RealityEngine graphics hardware [S1, unofficial]. It was designed to provide interactive frame rates for volumetric datasets by exploiting the hardware's ability to perform trilinear interpolation in parallel across textured polygons [S1, unofficial][S4]. The approach was detailed in early literature on hardware-accelerated volume rendering, where it served as a primary alternative to software ray casting and early hardware-specific volume rendering units [S1, unofficial]. It is widely used in medical imaging and scientific visualization where interactive performance on standard graphics hardware is required [S4].
